title: Louisville & Nashville Railroad Co. v. Mottley (1908)
summary: The contract claim did not arise under federal law merely because the plaintiffs anticipated a federal statutory defense and challenged that defense constitutionally.
notes:
The existence of a federal question somewhere in a lawsuit does not answer § 1331. Grable supplies a distinct and limited route for a federal issue necessarily embedded in the plaintiff’s own state-law claim. It does not erase Mottley’s defense rule.

The Mottleys were injured in an 1871 railway accident and settled for lifetime free passes; a 1906 federal act forbade free passes and the railroad refused renewal in 1907. They sought specific performance; the trial court overruled the railroad's demurrer and ruled for them, and the Supreme Court raised the jurisdictional defect on its own motion and directed dismissal.

sections.Parties: The Mottleys sued the railroad to enforce an agreement providing passes for transportation. The railroad resisted further performance after federal legislation restricted free passes.
sections.Material Facts: The passes formed part of a settlement of the Mottleys’ earlier injury claims. When the railroad stopped renewing them, the Mottleys asserted their contractual entitlement. Their complaint anticipated that the railroad would rely on the federal statute and argued that the statute either did not apply or would be unconstitutional if applied to their agreement. Those federal arguments answered an expected defense to the contract claim.
sections.Procedural History: The federal trial court ruled on the controversy. On appeal, the Supreme Court examined subject-matter jurisdiction and directed dismissal because the case did not fall within the statutory federal-question grant. Later litigation concerning the merits is a separate episode noted by the casebook.
sections.Issue: Did the anticipated federal defense and the plaintiffs’ constitutional response make the action one arising under federal law?
sections.Holding: No. Federal-question jurisdiction had to appear as part of the plaintiffs’ own properly pleaded claim, rather than in an anticipated defense or reply.
sections.Reasoning: The legal source of the asserted right was the agreement settling the earlier dispute. Proving that claim did not itself require pleading a federal right. The possible federal restriction arose because the defendant would invoke it to resist liability. Allowing anticipated defenses to confer jurisdiction would make the forum depend on speculation about how the defendant might litigate and would expand the statutory grant beyond the well-pleaded complaint rule. The Court’s attention to the issue despite the merits proceedings also demonstrates the independent importance of federal subject-matter authority.

learning.why: The contract claim did not arise under federal law merely because the plaintiffs anticipated a federal statutory defense and challenged that defense constitutionally.

topics.cp-well-pleaded: A federal issue expected in the defense or a reply to that defense does not satisfy the well-pleaded complaint rule. A federal defense to a contract claim does not automatically convert that claim into a federal cause of action.
topics.cp-federal-question: The plaintiffs’ own claim arose from a settlement contract.
topics.cp-subject-matter: The Supreme Court examined federal jurisdiction even without relying on a party’s objection.
topics.cp-usc-1331: Mottley is the leading construction of the 'arising under' language of the federal-question statute.
topics.cp-statute-interpretation: The case is the standard example that the statutory 'arising under' grant is narrower than the Article III grant, and that courts raise subject-matter defects sua sponte.
